source_title: Is Apple's new iPad mini becoming too expensive for its own audience? - The Times of India
source_excerpt: Apple's smallest iPad has just received one of its biggest upgrades. It has also become considerably more expensive. At Rs 82,900, the new iPad mini raises an uncomfortable question: how much are consumers willing to pay for the convenience of a compact tablet?The latest model, announced on Monday, brings an OLED display, a powerful A20 Pro processor, improved connectivity and water resistance. On paper, it represents a substantial improvement over its predecessor. But the price changes the conversation.The previous iPad mini, launched in October 2024, started at Rs 49,900 in India. The new model costs Rs 33,000 more, representing an increase of about 66%. The Wi-Fi and cellular variant starts at Rs 1,00,900, taking Apple's smallest tablet past the psychological Rs 1 lakh mark. Thatâs just a lot of money for the iPad mini. Heck, itâs a lot of money for any iPad.For a product historically valued for its portability and relatively accessible entry point into the iPad ecosystem, that is a significant shift.Big upgrades, bigger price tagApple has a persuasive argument for the increase. The new 8.5-inch OLED screen promises richer colours, deeper blacks and better contrast than the LCD panel on the previous generation. Peak brightness reaches 1,200 nits, while thinner bezels allow Apple to increase screen size without substantially enlarging the device.The new mini is also thinner, measuring 5.4mm, and gains IP67-rated protection against water and dust.Inside, the A20 Pro chip delivers substantial performance improvements. Apple claims up to 60% faster multithreaded CPU performance, 2.7 times faster graphics and 4.5 times better AI performance compared with the previous generation.There is support for Wi-Fi 7, a landscape-oriented 12MP front camera, faster charging and Apple's latest intelligence features. These are meaningful improvements, particularly for users who intend to keep their tablets for several years.The iPad mini occupies an unusual position in Apple's portfolio. Its attraction is precisely what limits it: the small screen.For reading, note-taking, travelling, casual gaming and accessing documents on the move, the mini can be an excellent companion. It fits into spaces where larger tablets become cumbersome and offers considerably more working room than a smartphone.Doctors using digital records, pilots accessing flight information, field workers and artists sketching on the move may find the form factor particularly useful. But these are relatively specialised requirements.For someone primarily watching videos, attending online classes, browsing websites or working on documents, a larger iPad may offer a more comfortable experience. A MacBook, meanwhile, remains better suited to sustained typing, complex spreadsheets and multitasking.That creates a difficult proposition for the new mini. At Rs 82,900, buyers are being asked to pay a considerable premium for a screen that is deliberately smaller than those on many less expensive tablets.Apple Pencil Pro costs Rs 11,900, pushing the combined price to Rs 94,800. Adding the new Rs 8,500 Smart Folio takes the package to Rs 1,03,300.Even the more affordable USB-C Apple Pencil adds Rs 7,900.For students, occasional creators and consumers seeking a secondary device, that is a substantial investment in a tablet that cannot fully replace a laptop.Is Apple testing the loyalty of mini users?Apple's pricing also reflects a broader change in its product strategy. Rather than positioning every smaller device as a more affordable alternative, the company increasingly treats compactness itself as a premium feature. Engineering a powerful processor, sophisticated display and advanced components into a smaller enclosure carries costs, but it also allows Apple to target customers willing to pay for a specific experience.This approach may work for the mini's loyal audience. Unlike larger tablets, where buyers can choose from numerous screen sizes and price points, the market for genuinely compact premium tablets remains limited. Apple therefore faces less direct competition for customers who specifically want a small, high-performance device.The 2024 iPad mini already offered strong performance, Apple Pencil support and access to Apple's extensive tablet app ecosystem. For many existing owners, the new display and processor may not dramatically change everyday tasks.There is also the question of artificial intelligence. Although Apple is emphasising the A20 Pro's capabilities, the usefulness of increasingly sophisticated on-device AI features will depend on how well they improve common activities, rather than merely how quickly the processor completes benchmark tests.Indian buyers are particularly sensitive to this distinction. Premium devices have an established audience, but a Rs 33,000 increase substantially narrows the pool of consumers who can justify an upgrade.Apple may be comfortable with that trade-off. The company does not necessarily need the mini to become a mass-market bestseller. A smaller group buying higher-priced devices could still support the product commercially.Whether that strategy strengthens the mini over time is another question.The new iPad mini is unquestionably more capable. Its OLED screen, lighter construction and improved processing power make it attractive for users who genuinely benefit from carrying a compact tablet.But for everyone else, the value proposition has weakened.At Rs 82,900, the iPad mini is no longer an easy recommendation as a convenient second screen. It is a specialised premium device whose size must be central to the buyer's needs. Apple has made its smallest iPad better than ever.
